utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we continue, Mr. Repinc, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to conclude your last 15 minutes of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I am, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday at the close of business, we were discussing your conclusions on the concept of the defence of populated areas, and you in fact -- you in fact in your evidence indicated that you relied on General Mrksic's directive of February 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: For the record, D944.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- as supporting your conclusions. Now, and you in fact, yesterday, specifically pointed out paragraph 5.11 as the section of that document that you relied on. General, I put it to you that the defence of populated areas as contemplated in that document is defence from outside the towns and not from within, as asserted by you. How do you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that what -- that I don't know what made you conclude that, given that defence of towns includes the defence of access routes to those towns and the towns themselves. This is explained in the rules of the former army, where, in cases of town defences, such as in the rules for brigades or other units, it is clearly stated how settlements are to be prepared for defence. Defending an access route to a town rather than defending the town itself as well, would be illogical, because if any forces were -- forced to withdraw or defeated, would have to take a different route, although both access routes and towns are legitimate targets in such cases. Therefore, I would not agree with you that a town is exclusively defended outside its boundaries; a town is also defended within -- from within.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could called 65 ter 3360 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You recall Mr. Kehoe showed you formats depicting the boundary lines of the Gospic Military District and the Split Military District as of 6th August and as of 14th August. I don't have to call those documents. You probably remember that, General, do you? Do you remember those documents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, I appreciate you may not have seen this document on the screen. This is it an order dated 16th August of General Gotovina. And I'll read the first few paragraphs. It says: "Due to the changed" -- I'm sorry. Before that, do you recall that in that chart as per those boundary lines drawn by the Defence as of 14th August, Gracac was outside the area of responsibility of Split Military District? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in this order dated 16th August, 1995, it says: "Due to the changed tactical and operational situation following the offensive operations of our forces, and in order to properly organise and execute the defence of the front line arrived at, I hereby order: The commanders of OG Otric and OG Sajkovic shall immediately organise a persistent and active defence on the line arrived at." Paragraph 2 reads: "OG Otric shall organise and execute an active and persistent defence in the zone, right. Planinica" - and then there's a trigger point given - "Stolinova Glava, Crijemusnjaka" - pardon my pronunciation - "all excluded and left Sjenica, trigger point 1113; Una railway station; Medak, trigger point 689; Veljko Sedlo, trigger point 1208; Gracac, all included." So do you note from this order of General Gotovina dated 16th August that, as of 16th August, Gracac is included in the area of responsibility of the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we take this order, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit P2705.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2705 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You read Medak, and I remember that we had already some problems in locating village Medak, compared to the Medak pocket, but here it reads both in the original and in the English translation Mededak, which seems to be a bit different.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, my apologises for the mispronunciation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, I want to draw your -- take you to paragraph 173 of your expert report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we could look at paragraph 173.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And there you report as follows: "The collective special police forces of the Ministry of the Interior formally turned over the border in the territory of Gornji and Donji Lapac to the units of the 118th Home Guard Regiment and the Gospic Military District's 8th Home Guard Regiment while the collective forces staff received an order." Now your citation is there to an order which has no reference to the special police handing over the borders of Gornji and Donji Lapac to the units of the Gospic Military District. So can you tell the Trial Chamber as to what your source of information is that on the 9th August - and that's -- your report is for the 9th August - the special police forces handed over that territory formally to the Gospic Military District, what are you relying on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I relied on a report drafted by General Markac for that day, which he sent to the Chief of Staff, General Cervenko, whereby it is stated that there had been a hand-over of that area. It says here Donji and Gornji Lapac, however, it is actually the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is to say, the area given to the Military District of Gospic. That was north of the railway station in Una. The Military District of Gospic introduced five Home Guard Regiments, and each one of them took over a certain portion of the area. The first area was taken by the 8th Home Guard Regiment, next 118th, 154th, 134th, and I think that was the sequence more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, now, you say there had been a handover of that area, it says here Gornji and Donji Lapac; however, it is actually the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now what you have reported here is that on 9th August, the special police forces handed over the -- you say the border in the territory of Gornji and Donji Lapac. Now where did you read that on the 9th August the special police forces handed over this territory? Now you're saying it's the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina but my question is with regard to Gornji and Donji Lapac. Where did you read that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I based that conclusion on the fact that the special police forces pulled out of that area and returned to their home units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you -- on the basis that the special police forces left the area on the 9th August, you presumed that there was a formal hand-over of the territory from the special police to the Gospic Military District?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was a formal hand-over, but one in real terms. If we try to look into the analysis of the commander of the Military District of Gospic concerning those facts - please bear with me. I'm looking for a reference concerning that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, my time is --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand it. I apologise for being unable to find it now. I would have to go through the material I have to come up with the exact reference pertaining to the report of the commander of the Gospic Military District.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But, General, in your answer just now, you just said -- this is what you say: "It wasn't a formal hand-over, but in real -- I don't think it was a formal hand-over but one in real terms." But you have -- what you have reported in paragraph 173 is that there was a formal hand-over. You say formally turned over. Now, are you withdrawing from that position, or have you made a mistake there in paragraph 173 with regard to the formal hand-over?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I have to apologise for that. This was a real hand-over. In Croatian when you say "formal," it may have a pro forma connotation; one can wonder whether it was done in full or not. Therefore, the issue would be whether such a hand-over was carried out in full or partially only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, just for my understanding, is it that you want to test the accuracy of the formal or not formal hand-over and the sources; or is there a challenge to the fact that the special police withdrew from that area and that other units here - Gospic Military District - took responsibility for this area? Is it the substance or is it accuracy, reliability, what we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The substance, Mr. President. We have not come across any evidence to show that the special police forces handed over the territory formally or in real terms to the Gospic Military District units, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We heard -- at least the testimony of some members of the special police, who said that at a certain moment they -- they left the area and returned to their own bases, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Some units, Mr. President. But there is evidence that -- that there was a base set up in Donji Lapac for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Until -- it's not exactly certain as to -- so I'm trying to inquire as to what this -- what General Repinc's source of information is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Since he has referred to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now it's at least clear to me what are you aiming at. Mr. Repinc.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, I finally found the document. This is the document analysis of Operation Storm, 1995, the Military District of Gospic command, dated the 30th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, if you could give us the footnote, we could call up that document on the screen. Footnote in your --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says footnote 105.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is 3D00641. You would like to have it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 7 of that document, concerning the activities of the 8th Home Guards Regiment --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is page 8 in e-court in Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the English version would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Page 8 in English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, could you draw our attention to the paragraph you relied on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The penultimate paragraph. However, it's not on this page. Yes, yes: "On the fourth day, a single regiment ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, a single battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I believe it's the next page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, can you please let us know which paragraph you're relying on to --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the penultimate paragraph, referring to the 8th Home Guards Regiment. "On the fourth day ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So as I understand your testimony to be, you read this paragraph as indicating that there has been a formal hand-over of the territory from the special police to the Gospic military police -- Gospic Military District units. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trying to say that the Military District of Gospic split the area into five areas: First we have the 8th; then the 118th Home Guards Regiment; and if we move to page 9, we see that the task that took place first was mopping up; and after that, they took up positions along the border. On that page, we have the 118th Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Which page are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 9 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That would be page 9 in e-court. I'm sorry, page 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, due to lack of time, is it correct, then, that the source you're relying on to support your report record in paragraph 173 that, on 9th August, the special police forces handed over this territory to the Gospic Military District unit, is this document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently English translation is not ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, I was on the wrong channel, Your Honours. Can the witness repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your answer because we missed the English translation. The question put to you by Ms. Mahindaratne was whether it was this document which was the source for your conclusion that, on 9th of August, the special police forces handed over the territory to the Gospic Military District. And we're talking about the area of Donji and Gornji Lapac and the state border nearby. Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The report of the commander of the Gospic Military District is one of these, and it states what its units were doing every day. It states that in that period of time, the units reached the state border; namely, 118th, in the region of Kulen Vakuf. This was confirmed in another document as well, namely the analysis of Operation Storm produced by the special police where, at page 18, it is stated that at 1400 hours on the 9th of August, members of the Home Guard Regiment handed over their positions in the general area of Kulen Vakuf, the villages Kalati, Ostrovica, suma Laniste, which is the unit that was deployed from Donji Lapac and moving toward Kulen Vakuf. At page 19, it is stated that the IKM -- the IZM, the forward command post of the special police in Ostrovica, ceased to exist. And the special police units were sent to their home units upon the order of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 614, page 18 and 19 in e-court, Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I missed the letter. Was it D or P?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: P, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, I was trying to find in these documents that you relied on a specific time-frame at which the special police handed over this territory to the Gospic Military District.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could have a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: English version of the e-court of document P614 relies on page 15. That is a data entered for 9 August, 1995, under the 1030 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry, 14 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which reads -- yes, because ... 14 hours reads: "Members of the Home Guard Regiment executed the hand-over of positions in the general area of Kulen Vakuf from Kalati village, Ostrovica village, the Laniste woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And on the next page is enter for 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness is supposed to give us the sources. It's -- it's appreciated that you point us to P641 [sic] as being the number of the document the witnesses apparently is referring to, but I think it's for the witness to tell us where he initially said page 18, page 19, that it is on another page that we find the answer to the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The witness was referring on hard copy documents page --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, do you have anything to add to this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't have the document on the screen, so I didn't intervene. But, as I said, based on the reports from the Gospic Military District, which clearly state that the units reached the state border and took control of it, and based on the report from the special police commander for the 9th of August, 1995, my conclusion is that the special police units left the area and returned to their home units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Based on that, would you then agree that if there was some form of hand-over on 9th August from special police forces to the Gospic Military District, then that territory was under the control of the special police forces from the point of capture of that territory until such hand-over?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for control, control was not exercised throughout the border areas taken by the Gospic Military District. Rather, it was the case only in relation to the area that was drawn in my report for that particular date, and that involved the general area of Kulen Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, I'm referring to paragraph 173 where you include the area of Gornji Lapac and Donji Lapac. My question to you is, If there is an formal hand-over of that territory on a specific date from special police to Gospic Military District units, then that would interfere, isn't it right or would you agree with me that up to such point of hand-over, that territory is within the control of the special police, otherwise an issue of handing over doesn't arise, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're going back to my earlier answers where I said that the special police was not competent to exercise control over the territories. As of the 7th of August, if we're talking about the area of Lapac, there weren't only special police units but also the 9th Guards and the 118th Home Guard Regiment, all of which were from the Gospic Military District, as well as others from that district.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: General, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I conclude my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mikulicic, I earlier tried to gently refrain from giving us the sources in this document, which pages. And then you said, Well, the witness is looking at the hard copy. Now, both in English and in B/C/S, the hard copy page numbering is exactly the same as in e-court, so, therefore, instead of just remaining silent, which, of course, is your right under those circumstances, I really have great difficulties in understanding how this could be an answer to my gentle effort to elicit from the witness the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, I think the pagination in hard copy and the e-court is not exactly the same. I think the difference is one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I have got for English page 15, that is page at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 15 in English gives as a page source at the top 15 out of 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, 15 is 15. Now, we have -- in the B/C/S version, I see paging numbering appearing at the top. Page 15 is ERN 0349-3610, which is, in the B/C/S, page 15 out of 51. Therefore -- and even if it would be one page different, then, of course, to -- if the witness says page 18, 19, to tell him that it is on 15, then even if there is one page number difference, then it still is covered by my observation, that we rather leave it to the witness to find the pages on which he relied. But since you did respond to what I said, I have great difficulties in understanding where the page differences are, unless you have a different e-court or different hard copies. Let's leave it behind us. It's not a dramatic matter. If I made a mistake, of course, I'm quite willing to -- not only to acknowledge that but even to apologise if I have been unfair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes it's really different to rely on hard copy, e-court copy, English version, B/C/S version, and above that, there is another version of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if I give guidance as who is to answer the question, who is to find the sources --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I respect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then you will understand that unknown copies of a different origin are not included in I -- and I think appropriately, I find my basis for my observations of what I see in e-court and what I see as images of what appear to be hard copies. Let's -- let's not spend any more time on it. The sequence at this moment, I did understand there is some need for further questions. Would it not be best if -- because -- that we first give an opportunity to the other Defence teams so that can you cover that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- area as well when re-examining the witness. Wouldn't that be the most logical sequence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, Mr. Kay? Unless you disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, no. No, it's fine. It's quite all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could bring back up on the screen P2705, which counsel showed you, which is the 16 August 1995 order by General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think it's P2705, 2705.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, this is the order that counsel showed to you. And as can you see in the preamble of the order, there's no reference to any order by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the second page, you can see -- I'm sorry -- if we can turn to the second page in B/C/S, please. And if I may, the third page in the B/C/S. I wanted the bottom, who this is being sent to. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you can see in that document that is not being -- has not been sent by General Gotovina to the Main Staff. So let us go back to the documents that I showed you the other day, and then show you yet another one. And if we could go back to D559, which is General Cervenko's order of 14 August, 1995, where he changed the areas of responsibility that we set forth in the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, as you can see in this document, of course, it has the filing number of 512-06-05/01, 95485. And on the last two pages of this order by General Cervenko, we have the Split Military District areas of responsibility set forth. And if you can could just -- I don't expect you to memorise it -- if you can keep that particular document identification number in mind, I would like to complete this and show you a document that has not been examined this morning. D1002, which is General Gotovina's order of 20 August, 1995. Now, General, would you agree with me that the first two lines of the preamble of this order refers back to General Cervenko's order of 14 August 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let us turn to -- to page 3 in the English, and -- frankly, I'm not certain what it is in the B/C/S, but it is after number 2. Go on to ... If we can go to the -- excuse me. Page 3 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn the page in the English, please. Can we turn the page in the English. There we go. In the middle of the page there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As you can see in point 2 in the areas of responsibility, General Gotovina tracks the areas of responsibility set forth in General Cervenko's order of the 14th of August, 1995, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, in this particular order, what we see is General Cervenko giving the order and then ultimately General Gotovina sends it down to his subordinates; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have nothing further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Yes, I changed the order a bit because in some respects it may be that questions are also addressing matters which were raised by the Prosecution. That's what I had on my mind. And since there seem to be no -- Mr. Kay, do you have any --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Then, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I think the proper sequence is, and that's not exactly what Rule 92 ter says, first of all: What's put on paper, does that reflect what was said? That's very factual. And the third issue is whether the witness, if same questions would be put to him today, whether he would give similar answers. Each of them gives a piece in the chain, which is there to establish the highest level of reliability of the written statement compared to the -- what is in the memory of the witness. Mr. Registrar. utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Penic, you told us that you are a lawyer and that you have a private practice in Zagreb in a law firm.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During the homeland war between 1990 and onwards --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, I apologise. I am being reminded that I should acquaint the public with the summary of Mr. Penic's statement. By your leave, I would like to do that now. It seems that I have difficulty getting acquainted with that part of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's still a list outstanding, Mr. Mikulicic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Penic is a lawyer currently working in his private practice in Zagreb. During the homeland war, he was an employee of the state administration. More precisely, between 1995 and 1999 he was assistant minister of justice in the field of criminal law. At the same time, he was secretary of the state commission for pardons. The Ministry of Justice took no part whatsoever in the creation of court practice, jurisprudence, or decisions made by the regular or military courts. It exerted no influence over the work of judges or prosecutors in any specific cases. The ministry carried out administrative tasks concerning the functioning of the judiciary. Mr. Penic, as assistant minister in the field of criminal law, worked on the various legal drafts pertaining to that area, including the Law on Pardon. Great effort was made to construct a modern judicial system of the newly created Republic of Croatia. After the occupied territories were liberated, courts were established. There were difficulties in their work, because during the occupation of those territories of Croatia, land registers and court registers were partially or completely destroyed, along with other types of court documents. Mr. Penic took part in the work of the state commission for pardons, which processed applications for pardon. After that commission was given the opinions of relevant prosecutors, they would submit entire files for final decision to the president of the state. The Croatian parliament also, on several occasions, adopted the Law on Pardons as well as different amendments to that law concerning crimes committed during the homeland war with the exception of war crimes. Mr. Penic, on several occasions as an employee of the Ministry of Justice, appeared before the media in the FRY, explaining the measures put in place by the Croatian state, vis-à-vis criminal liability of the rebelled Serb population in the territory of Croatia, as well as concerning the issues of pardon and amnesty in terms of criminal proceedings. This concludes the summary of Mr. Penic's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Penic, I would kindly ask you to briefly explain to us what your work was in the Ministry of Justice, focussing on the specific area of your work.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: After so many years, it is difficult for me to explain that, also coupled with the fact that I'm in a completely different field nowadays. It is difficult for me to be precise, especially in terms of dates and numbers. However, I recall very well something that was important to all of us at the time, i.e., all the priorities we worked on and the dynamics of the processes. I recall the period when I arrived the Ministry of Justice, after having worked in the State Prosecutor's office. The entire state administration was being structured and created. In the Ministry of Justice, at the time, there was a new administration for criminal law that was being established. I was put at the helm of it as assistant minister for criminal law. At the time, as well as today, I believe, it had a separate department for pardons and a department for criminal regulation. I was appointed by the Croatian government as an expert and professional in the field, tasked with providing professional opinion and processing of pardon applications so as to prepare the files to be put before the state commission for pardons. In other words, I carried out a professional administrative work. I believe at that time and under those circumstances, we were able to provide some quality work. On the other hand, during that time, Croatia took over much of the legislation of the former state, which disintegrated. Once our courts and other judicial bodies were set up, they followed that regulation, which was inherited from the former state. Our task at that time was to prepare and draft a legislative framework and specific regulations which would be originally Croatian, if I may say so. In that regard, expert Working Groups were established within the Ministry of Justice, which worked as part of the administration that I was the head of and with its support. Some prominent professionals were included from the judiciary, the academic circles, and so on and so forth. That body proposed a number of laws in the criminal field to the Croatian government and, afterwards, the parliament. This included the Law on Criminal Procedure, the criminal law, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Penic, tell us something about the relationship between the Ministry of Justice and the judiciary, the presidents of courts and judges who performed their duties.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: From my immediate experience, I can tell you that given the separation of power in Croatia into the three branches of government, we, in the Ministry of Justice, were, de facto, a service at the disposal of the prosecutor's offices and courts. The ministry, not directly my administration but the administration for organisational and personnel matters, was charged with providing all the necessary conditions for unimpeded work of the courts. There was no possibility for us as employees of the Ministry of Justice to participate in the work of the courts and, God forbid, to have any sort of involvement with case files. It was our task to be their administrative, technical, and any other support required for them in order to do their work properly under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Penic, let me go back to transcript, page 28, line 11, where you said that the Ministry of Justice didn't have any powers in relation to the courts. And you said the word -- you mentioned the term "de facto." Did you use another Latin term?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: De jure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Penic, you told us that you also performed the duty of secretary in the state commission for pardons. In what way did the commission work? What was the procedure applied in the work of the commission?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: In my view, at the time, there was a general shortage of lawyers and professionals in general. Since I was at the head of the administration for criminal law, it came about - I don't know in which way - that the following procedure was put in place. Since I was assistant minister for -- of justice for criminal law, I was also appointed secretary of the commission for pardons. This was to ensure that the administration for criminal law headed by me and in charge of the business related to pardons would have continuity in its work, consistency in its work. It involved human destinies, human tragedies, these were applications arriving from individuals who, for various reasons and under various circumstances, came to be perpetrators of crimes or accessories thereof. Specifically, when we received an application for pardon, the law allowed to us forward such an application directly to the president of the state. However, the president would return the files to the Ministry of Justice, because we were in charge of processing them. We would categorise these applications by the category of crimes, their gravity, and occasionally according to the location where they were committed. We tried to react promptly, be efficient, and not waste undue time. We would send these files to the courts seized of these cases, because this was dictated by the law for their opinion. We also sent them to state prosecutors and law -- for their opinion. If the individuals applying for pardon were serving their sentences, we would also seek the opinion of prison authorities. Based on all of the foregoing, we would put together a file containing all the evidence and documents. And complete with the opinion of the minister of justice, the file would be sent to the commission, which, at its meetings, would issue very specific recommendations to the president of the state, if and why certain individuals should be pardoned. For the most part, the president of the state would adopt these regulations. I don't think if there is anything else you are interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me just put another question to you before the break. In the period between 1992 and 1995, to the best of your recollection, what was the ethnic make-up of the applicants for pardon?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Well, there were all sorts. I don't want you to hold me to the numbers that I give you. But most of them, most of the applications for pardons, came from members of the paramilitary Serb units, predominantly these were individuals of Serb ethnicity. I think that two thirds were actually them, so that would be the ratio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this would be a convenient moment for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break. Before we do so, however, I'm still, Mr. Mikulicic, my -- I'm a bit slow on my mind now and then. We had a look at this entry of 1400 hours on -- in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is in the -- progressed on the sixth day of Operation Storm, hand-over of positions in the general area of Kulen Vakuf from Kalati village, Ostrovica village, and the Laniste woods. Is my understanding correct - and I'm addressing both parties - that Kulen Vakuf is in Bosnia, not in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Kalati is in Bosnia, is not in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's -- that place is almost strictly based on the border between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So it's a border area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a border area. Then Ostrovica village is also close to Kulen Vakuf but still on Bosnian territory; is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, of that village, I'm not certain, Your Honour, but I could check --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could check on maps, perhaps that we have a proper understanding of whether the hand-over of positions was referred to by using names of villages in Bosnia or by using names of villages in Croatia. And, to be quite honest, if you could locate the Laniste woods, that would certainly assist the Chamber further in understanding the document and the testimony of the last witness. With this invitation to the parties, we will have a break, Mr. Penic, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I again apologise for the late start. But meetings during the break took more time than expected. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as it refers to the discussion immediately before the break, I have a map, which was already in the evidence, on which we can find places like Ostrovica, Kalati, but we cannot find Laniste woods. It is not on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Well then we are facing similar problems that the villages are mentioned on the maps; the woods are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- well, then at least we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just for further assistance, the three places, Kulen Vakuf, Ostrovica, and Kalati are all close by. Ostrovica is around nine kilometres east of Donji Lapac across the border, if that can help find it on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I found the others on the map, just not Laniste. And I just wanted to be sure that I was looking at the same villages as the parties think I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So I think the best source is P190.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Penic, let us go back to the discussion we had before the break concerning pardons. Which were the crimes involving the applicants for pardon who were ethnic Serbs taking part in the armed rebellion that were granted pardons, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: For the most part, these were crimes committed in the war, during the war, and related to the war. I think that in the highest of percentages, the crime was participation, aiding and abetting in an armed rebellion, and failure to respond to a military call-up. These, were for the most part, the crimes involved when it came to pardon, with the exception of the crimes that were under the law, the ones which were the gravest crimes, and they were namely war crimes and the crime of genocide.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Mikulicic please repeat the number he is seeking to be called up. The interpreter could not catch up that speedily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number you wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- call up Mr. Mikulicic, could you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will repeat, Your Honour. [Interpretation] The number is 3D00292, and we it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is the decision granting the pardon to convicts from the month of November 1992, that's to say, the 10th of November. To the best of your knowledge, at what point in time did the procedure commence of the issuing of decisions granting pardon?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was immediately following the so-called log revolution, that's to say, the month of August of 1990. Or 1991; I'm not sure. I know that I was on my way home from the Adriatic trying to avoid logs. So it was right from the start of the armed rebellion that the decisions granting pardon applied to, in terms of the individuals taking part in the armed rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As an illustration, let us look at the top part of this decision relating to Petar Novogradic, which states that he been convicted to two years in prison for the crime of preparing armed rebellion under Article 236. Is that, in fact, the crime you referred to just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For reference to Their Honours, the total of 104 persons were covered by these applications; 35 of them were granted pardon for -- and they participated in armed rebellion; and 23 had their applications rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] could I have a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1936. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1936 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let us call up document number 3D00291.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That earlier decision granted partial pardon for the serving of the sentence. This particular decision, dating from end of 1992 relating to 24 persons, pardon is granted, or that's to say, immunity from criminal prosecution. Is this the way, Mr. Penic, in which pardon was granted both to those who were already convicted and those who had yet to be prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Pardons applied to persons who were yet to be prosecuted and those who had already been convicted alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this number be -- could this document be granted a number, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections from Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1937. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1937 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a reference to Their Honours, 24 persons were covered by this decision, all of them for the crime of armed rebellion. Can we call up 3D00294, please.

Again, dating from the end of 1992, covering 50 individuals. Mr. Penic, as far as you remember, was this sort of decision issued as part of the procedure you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC

If Mr. Mikulicic wants to bar table them, we will not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Penic, you've described for us the way in which the pardoning procedure functioned. In addition to this procedure, there was another procedure applied, pursuant to the Law on Pardons. I will ask you to give us your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before that, can we call up 3D00287, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document, can you tell us, Mr. Penic, which legal area was regulated by the Law on Pardons from criminal prosecution for the offences in -- committed in armed conflicts and in Croatia -- in the war against Croatia? This was dated September 1992.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: These laws on pardons, in relation to the crimes committed in the war against Croatia, expressed the will on the part of the legislation and the government on the Croatia - as an aside, just let me tell you that this document -- this law had been widely covered in the press and had been widely publicly debated -- the will to -- to express the will for all those members of the Serb paramilitary units who had not been involved in the commission the gravest of crimes, such as war crimes, to have these crimes pardoned. I'm speaking for myself now, but I'm sure that this was, at the time, a general assessment and view of the public at large. In other words, the individuals who were misled and who had been manipulated, in a way, were to be shown in this way through a piece of legislation that the government and the legislature wanted not to sanction, such actions that followed from manipulative policies of leaderships, unless these actions involved the commission of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us look at Article 1 of the law. As we can see, it relates to the time-period from the 17th of August, 1990, up to the effective date of the proclamation of the law. It is stated that criminal prosecution shall not be undertake against the perpetrators of crimes in the war against Croatia. And where criminal proceedings have already been initiated, they would be suspended by the court ex officio. If a person, subject to the amnesty stipulated in this law, has been held in custody or in remand, the court shall order that the person be released. And, as you said, this law also states that it does not relate to the perpetrators of crimes for which the Republic of Croatia has its obligations under international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this document be assigned a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections from the Prosecution. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1938. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the same case applies here as with pardons, and that's to say that we have four more documents related to the Law on Amnesty where time-limits were changed because the law had been amended on three occasions until 1996. Shall we apply the same procedure, Mr. President, here as well and tender these documents from a bar table, or else we can go through them. It won't take more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a bit confused, but perhaps that's my lack of understanding, that -- let me just check. Yes, so you would say that time-limits for amnesty were changed in subsequent legislation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think for this topic I think there is only two or three more. If we just go through briefly with the witness, just to point out the dates. And we can just admit them all at once at the end. But I think it may be usual for the Chamber to have the dates as we go along, rather than bar table these particular ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I agree with my learned colleague, Your Honour, and that will not take us many time. At most --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because, you say -- yes, let me ... Yeah, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Can the Registrar call up 3D00288, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document, I wish to direct your attention to the fact that the first Law on Amnesty covered the period between 17th of August and the date of the proclamation of the law, which was the month of September 1992. What we're seeing now is the law that had amended the previous law. In Article 1, the date of application is now the 10th of May, 1995; that's in Article 1, as the ending date. So the entire period has been covered starting from 1990 through to the 10th of May, 1995. Mr. Penic, can you comment on the change -- on the methodology of amending legislation?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. But if I can just, as an aside, say this. Since I took part in the expert group working on this, it seemed to us very important at the time that the legislation is passed which states that the court would, ex officio, release someone who is held somewhere or in the process of something. So the rationale behind this was that there would be no discussion or debate, that there would be no random assessment made, that the court would have an ex officio obligation to apply the law. On the other hand, how long the war would go on for was still an unknown. It was an assessment based on the involvement of the international community that the law -- that the war would end in 1992. Unfortunately, that was not the case, and that's why the law mentioned -- was adopted in 1992. Under the law making procedure, it was the easiest solution to stipulate the length of its application in Article 1 and extend it to the 10th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can this document be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection from Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D1939. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1939 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] thank you, Mr. President. Let us now look at 3D00289.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is another Law on Amnesty, which was passed on the 21st of May, 1996. Again, the time-limit of its application was prolonged to the 1st of June, 1996, as stipulated in Article 1. Can we have a brief comment of yours in relation to the provision where the amnesty is stipulated for citizens who have a residence in the temporarily occupied areas of Vukovar, Srijem, and Osijek-Baranja counties. Why are these two counties specifically mentioned in Article 1 of the law?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: It was a time-period of a peaceful reintegration of that area into Croatia. The effort was to launch various initiatives aimed towards bringing about a peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia. And the effort was successful, and it is believed that the law gave its contribution to that end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be assigned a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D1940.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in the absence of any objections, is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last document we have in this batch has already been admitted as D680, and I would like to call it up. This is the Law on General Amnesty, dated the 24th of September, 1996. Article 1, again, provides for the period of its application; namely, from the 17th of August, 1990, through to the 23rd of August, 1996. Article 2 expressly provides for the way in which the law is to be applied. In other words, the perpetrators would not be criminally prosecuted. In para 2, where proceedings have been launched, they will be suspended. And in para 3, if the person has been taken into custody, the person would be released by order of a court. In Article 3, the law expressly lays down the crimes which are the subject of this law and those which are not. Mr. Penic, can we have comments from you on this law.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: I can certainly provide a comment, although I don't know what the limits of my testimony are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead but briefly.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: I personally participated in the drafting of these laws, and I was witness to much discussion that took place, since they were proclaimed in the time of war and aggression against Croatia when my family still lived in Vukovar and at the time when the Croatian public was highly sensitive about the issue. Despite all that, both the Croatian public and the parliament as well as Croatian authorities and policy makers put such regulations in place. It is my deep conviction that this presented an enormous step forward to try, under the circumstances prevailing, to forget and forgive, to the extent possible. It is not because I participated in the drafting of these laws that I say that I believe them to be sound legislation. I apologise if I have gone off on a tangent a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document. Sorry, no, it's already in evidence; apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. If we could just -- there's a, I think, translation issue with this document or at least, of course, I can't be sure. But if we go to the previous page in English, Article 1, and the reason I noticed it is we had a translation from the Markac against before they realised it was in evidence. And at Article 1, in the next-to-last line in the English, where it says: "Armed rebellion or armed conflict or related to aggression, armed rebellion, or armed conflicts." I think there's also another version where that last -- that next to last "or" was an "and." "And related to aggression, armed rebellion, or armed conflicts in the Republic of Croatia." I know there have been other witnesses that have touched on this topic. I don't think it's crucial, but I just wanted to draw the Chamber's attention on the fact that there is this uncertainty in two translations that we've received. And I don't know if we should just send it to review or ask the witness to clarify which one, if it's an "and" or an "or" that should be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: From Markac point -- from Markac Defence point, the proper translation should be "and," not "or."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to understand here the difference between the two. And we have two times the word "or," between armed rebellion and armed conflicts. Would, in both cases --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, it's the other one. There's two groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There's the first group with the ors, and then there's the second group also with an or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And so it's the middle of the three ors we find on the third line of Article 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the one. Okay, now I fully understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps we should deal with any doubts concerning this issue and ask the witness to interpret para 1 of Article 1, since he took part in the drafting of this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Penic, Article 1 states in Croatian: "This law shall grant general amnesty from criminal prosecution and proceedings against perpetrators of criminal acts committed during aggression, armed rebellion, or armed conflicts and related to aggression, armed rebellion, or armed conflict in the Republic of Croatia?" In the Croatian version, we see two small i's, at least in the version I have, which, obviously --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: An armed rebellion represents an act of rallying and sporting weapons, which is one act under the law. And actually firing the weapons is another under the law. In any case, we wanted to include both in the amnesty under this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, then, the two i's in the Croatian version should actually be "and." So cumulatively. It is obvious that in the original text of the law there was a typographical error which caused the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit lost, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm. [Interpretation] Mr. President, Article 1 of the Law on General Amnesty, the second line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the Croatian word "oruzanum pobunam [phoen]," towards the end of the line you can see two small i's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is one too many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I understand. The one question remaining with the "or" and the "and" is, finally you say it's both, crimes committed during and crimes committed in relation. Now, is that a -- that would mean that if I do steal a cow from my neighbour during aggression, that that would fall within the terms of the amnesty as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The most classical type of crime known to all of us is something that was not included. Hence, my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it should be "during and in relation to"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I do not know what ii, whether that's -- first of all, it should be i. And then I do not know whether it's "and" or "or" in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It should be "i," and it's "and."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now it is perfectly clear to me. Please proceed. Could you then, the translation, as we have it on our screen now, could that be -- this is the translation prepared by -- because this one says "or."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that is wrong. Should be -- instead of "or," should be "and."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now who is responsible for this translation, so -- because we can't change a translation which is prepared by CLSS without having them review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It seems that it's a -- it's an OTP translation, so we will take care of having revised and corrected it and it sent around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Before we get to that, if we could consult during the break, because I'm not sure that we agree with the position that it should be an and. I have looked at the original now in the Croatian -- official Croatian legal database and it -- unfortunately, in the original, uses the ii.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I have got no idea whether ii stands for something else than i.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, here's the problem: In Croatian, if it's simply an extra i was typed, then it means "and;" it means just i. If it's that the L between the two i's was inadvertently dropped, then it would be ili which would be or.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which we find elsewhere in this line. We find ili once, and then you would say that -- if the parties could try to agree. And once I'm retired, I will start studying linguistics somewhere. Let's see, but is there any chance that anyone interprets -- if it would be a real "or," then my example, just given, stealing a cow of your neighbour, would fall within the scope of the amnesty. Is that the position of the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I must confess, I was looking for the law, so I wasn't following the exact question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I said before if -- is it the position -- if the Gotovina Defence leaves it open that it is still "or," the middle of the three, before the word "related to," whether it's "or related to," would it be the position of the Gotovina Defence that -- let me just check now. Yes, if that would still -- well, if there would still be a possibility that the word in dispute would be "or," that would mean that both crimes during armed conflict, aggression, et cetera, and crimes committed in relation to, they all would be covered by the amnesty laws. Which would mean that a cow being stolen during armed conflict from your neighbour would fall within the scope of this amnesty as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is our position, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Meaning either in the aggression or in an armed conflict. And if you wish, I can explain in detail, but I don't think it would be appropriate at this moment -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think at this moment. But then, at least, the position of -- so better commit a crime during aggression if you have any hopes for amnesty. This is not related to Croatia but in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I can give you the full background, Mr. President. This has already been at length discussed with Mrs. Rehn as to why it would have covered both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I must admit that I have no clear recollection at this moment. But I will immediately check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And it has been noticed by Mr. Bajic as well, on the record. While we're putting sources of evidence on the record, I want to do that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's please proceed at this moment. We've spent enough time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just for your reference, it could be of help, paragraph 2 of the Article 3 of that law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will have a look at it, and I will check both the sources just mentioned by the parties. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Penic, the last topic, in your statement, you say that, as an employee of the Ministry of Justice, you appeared on TV Vinkovci which is a Croatian TV station but that you also travelled to Belgrade to acquaint those interested with the contents of the Law on General Amnesty. Can you tell us something more about this activity of yours and what it was motivated by?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: I was at the collegium of the Ministry of Justice, given that this fell within the competence of my administration, to interpret the law and explain the Law on General Amnesty to them and to everyone else who wanted to know about it. I visited the Danubian region on several occasions, and I appeared in two TV broadcasts of a Croatian TV station, although they covered a wide area even outside Croatian territory. I was tasked to explain in lay terms what the provisions of this law entailed, and I was open to any questions by the viewers. One broadcast was interesting in particular. I recall that there were no provocations during the broadcast, which surprised me. And the interest that was shown was rather high. It is obvious that even those who could recognise themselves as falling under the provisions of that this law had a justified and bona fide interest in seeing how they could be included in its application. I was also part of a Croatian delegation which visited Belgrade on two occasions. Two of the representatives of the FRY who were present there from their ministry of foreign affairs as well as in the presence of our Ambassador to the FRY and in the presentation of their Ministry of Justice representatives as well as the representatives of an association founded by Mr. Savo Strbac, a former judge who had fled to the FRY. We were there to explain the provisions of this law in detail and provide interpretations. However, no matter how hard we tried, no matter how many times we tried to explain why this law was enacted, trying to say that anyone who had not committed a crime can return to Croatia, still, it was not taken up in practice. I don't know whether this was intentional or unintentional. But it seemed to me that they persistently refused to understand. In some radio broadcast in Croatia, I also explained this topic and provided interpretations of this law on behalf of the Ministry of Justice and the minister of the justice as well as the Republic of Croatia in general and its authorities, trying to say that all those who had not committed war crimes and certain most serious crimes can freely come back and would receive amnesty for anything they had done while being influenced by the policies at the time. Every time they were by the logs or doing anything of the sort. However, I'm not sure we received the exact reaction we were hoping for. This is what I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Penic, I thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Has any arrangement been made who goes first?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour. I'll go next, with the Court's leave, if that is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so. You will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay, Mr. Penic. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Penic, after Operation Storm and the liberation of Knin, were you aware of an agreement signed between the Croatian government, on one side, and the United Nations, through Mr. Akashi, on the other side? It's often called the Akashi-Sarinic Agreement.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Within the Ministry of Justice, were you ever provided a copy of that agreement to consider its content?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The minister of justice at that time was a Mr. Separovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And within your ministry, was he the government official who was the person you reported to?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: I was directly answerable to the minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware if Mr. Separovic had been given or provided with the Akashi-Sarinic Agreement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Whether he was aware of it or not is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to discuss one of the terms of the Akashi-Sarinic Agreement with Mr. Separovic concerning war criminals suspected of being within the UNCRO camp in Knin?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes. I discussed that with Mr. Separovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you've been telling us this morning about your role, in relation to alleged war criminals within the Croatian justice system. Was it for that reason that this matter was discussed with you concerning alleged war criminals in the UN camp?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Any discussions with me about the document itself and the way it was drafted and the reasons behind it is something that did not take place. Minister Separovic did, however, acquaint me in detail what the document contained and what was decided for me to do in the course of its implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I now want to look at that in a little bit more detail. How soon after the liberation of Knin did Mr. Separovic discuss with you the issue of the suspected war criminals in the UNCRO camp?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: In the period between 48 and 72 hours, after that, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And perhaps you can describe what happened. How did he discuss this with you; and what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: During Operation Storm, we were all called back to the Ministry of Justice to our offices. Those of us were male fell under the so-called work obligation, and we were there at the disposal. Minister Separovic summoned us to his office, and he told us that an agreement was concluded between Mr. Sarinic and Mr. Akashi, pursuant to which the Croatian side, as a precondition for about 1.000 refugees who were in the UN camp in Knin, to have them released, wanted to retain some 70 persons, I believe. It was believed that they were war crimes perpetrators. Under the agreement, Croatia was entitled to keep those people and put them in custody; whereas, all the others would be released. Minister Separovic told me that he had documents which came from the relevant State Prosecutor's offices and courts, amounting to the information which sustained reasonable doubts of those persons having committed war crimes. He gave me those documents, which I reviewed. It was my task to take those court files and documents to the UN camp in Knin and to serve those documents on those who were suspected of having committed war crimes. They had to sign off for their receipt, putting in place the possibility of meeting the precondition for the implication of the Akashi-Sarinic Agreement. Those suspects were supposed to be kept in custody, while others were supposed to be released, to go their different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I just want to look at one aspect of the answer you gave there, and it was towards the end of your statement where -- I will read out from the transcript: "Minister Separovic told me that he had documents which came from the relevant State Prosecutor's offices and courts, amounting to the information which sustained reasonable doubts of those persons having committed war crimes." It is the phrase "sustained reasonable doubts" that I wanted you to consider, as to whether you meant that, or what was your in your mind when you used that phrase "sustaining reasonable doubt." And I put that to you as a lawyer, as something you should consider.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes. Reasons to suspect was a category which, under the then Croatian law, as is now the case, which provided a possibility for conducting criminal investigative measures and investigations against certain persons. In order for a prosecutor to decide such -- to launch such an investigation, the relevant prosecutor needed to have documents which would provide for reasonable grounds of suspecting those people of having committed that. These were court decisions on launching investigations on keeping persons in custody or issuing warrant -- arrest orders. In any case, such a category was necessary, because it -- such material had to be beyond any doubt so as to be able to use as grounds to initiate any type of criminal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want -- now want to look at the files you were given by Minister Separovic and the type of documentation that was in those files that you reviewed. Perhaps you could describe that to the Court, the kind of documents you were looking at.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: These were documents originating from several courts located in the war areas, primarily Sibenik, Split, and Zadar. These were decisions passed down by the investigating judges of these courts and decisions, which I saw copies of only, citing the names of individuals and the crimes against them, their particulars. They contained the description, the factual description, of actus reus, the action committed, the legal qualification of the act, and the supporting evidence underpinning the request for investigation and the decision to launch an investigation. These were witness statements wherever witnesses were alive to tell the story. They contained crime scene investigation reports, interviews with either eye-witnesses or individuals who had knowledge or information of it. At any rate, the document had to be of a certain legal format. It had to meet all the legal elements and prerequisites in order for it to be the basis for prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you give a long answer, I'm allowing time for the translation to take place, Mr. Penic, so don't worry if I'm --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... silent. Now, again, the type of crimes that were within those files Minister Separovic gave you. Can you recollect what sort of crimes were alleged by the suspects?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Rape; driving out of civilians; torching their homes. These were the categories of offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, moving on from there, you were given the instruction to go to Knin with the files. So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: I was taken there by a professional driver. The practical arrangement was such that I was supposed to report to Mr. Cermak in Knin. He was supposed to receive me there, to find lodging for me, and to take me to the base so that I could formally turn over the documentation. I set out for Knin. General Cermak received me there in the company of another associate of his. I was put up in the house where he himself stayed. He took me in his car; I think it was a military vehicle, and accompanied me to the gate, to the UNCRO base in Knin.
