It was the UNCRO's representatives who then took me into the camp or into the base, into a room there, where I told them what my task was. I presented them with a copy of all these documents. Based on what I was told, they knew who these particular individuals were. And so I asked them to bring these individuals over to me so I could carry out the task that I was sent from Zagreb for. At that point there was commotion, some sort of rebellion or protest from these individuals. My powers were somewhat limited. I was not there as part of a member of the gendarmerie or as a policeman nor did you have powers to issue anyone with orders. I took a retreating stance, so to speak. I asked them once more to heed me. UNCRO representatives or UNPROFOR representatives, whatever they were called, were told that this was my task which I had to perform. I told them that I was not aware of what the status of all these individuals at the base was and that I didn't have any other instructions. I am coming back to what you initially asked me about, if I may, because I, indeed, did not see the Separovic-Akashi Agreement; I wasn't involved in it. My role was to implement it in that particular element, where individuals suspected of having committed war crimes were supposed to be retained. By happenstance, I didn't manage to hand over the documentation. I left in the company of UNCRO or UNPROFOR representatives who escorted me out of the camp. Mr. Cermak was waiting for me there. He took me back to his house where I relayed to him what had happened. He contacted Zagreb. And, in fact, I returned to Zagreb without having done what I was supposed to do there to begin with. Once I told Cermak what had happened, he contacted Zagreb, and then, as I returned to Zagreb on the following day, I was told again by the minister of justice that I should venture to go to Knin once more and that I would be accompanied by Vesna Skare Ozbolt as a representative of the office of the President of the state and as a representative of Mr. Separovic himself, as a person who would be on a higher position than myself, as a politician, who was Sarinic's right hand at the time. She returned to Knin with me, and she helped, in fact, with her resolute and decided stance and with her excellent command of English through conversation also with UNPROFOR representatives there to persuade the individuals involved to receive the documentation we were supposed to turn over to them. However, there were some 10 to 20 of them who persisted in their refusal to be served the documentation. I made a record of this, the names of the individuals and the date, stating that the individual concerned was officially told what the charges against him or her were and that in the -- in my presence, the presence of Madam Skare Ozbolt and the representatives of the international community, the individual was duly informed of it, whereby it was considered that the individual had been informed of the charges and of his rights and obligations. In a nutshell, that's what happened in relation to the hand-over of documentation, the serving of documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That was -- thank you. That was a very full answer. And in relation to your dealings with this matter, did Mr. Cermak have any authority over you at all? Was he, in any way, your superior in relation to what you were doing in your attempts to serve the documents?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cermak had absolutely nothing to do with it whatsoever. He was my host, who was, evidently, tasked with receiving me, taking care of my security and safety, finding accommodation with me, and accompanying me to the base. He did not even go into the compound with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to look at a document with you now, which is not yet a Court exhibit. It's 2D15-0018. It's a document dated the 19th of September, 1995, from the ministry of law, or justice, and it's a document signed by you and also sent to Minister Separovic. But it's written to Mr. Sarinic of the Office of the President of the Republic. I just want you to look at this document. And if you could read the first page. First of all, if you could tell me whether you've seen this document in the last 15 years or so before.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Could I see the end of the document as well, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Please turn to page 2. Page 2 in the English as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not the end. That's a list of a sort. In English, we do have the end, but not in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's page 2 of the Croatian, if we may have that, which is the end of the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's my signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And if you could just read through the second page.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: I don't recall the document, the text as such. What I do remember, though, is that once I've finished my dealings there, as I described them, I did write a report, and that must be it. I'm not challenging its authenticity. I didn't read it since, but, obviously, it confirms the better part of what I told you earlier on, as you can see. To my surprise, I do not recall Mr. Slobodan Lang being there, although he is a good friend of mine. That must be because of the lapse of time. From this document of mine, it follows that I acted on Mr. Sarinic's instructions conveyed to me by Minister Separovic, because, as you can see, at the end of the document, I am informing him of what I had done and that I had written a report on this issue to Mr. Sarinic. Now, what the follow-up was on my report and what the subsequent fate of these individuals was and how many of them had been detained and how many had been released, how many are still serving their sentences in Croatian prisons today, I don't know. What I do know is that, following this operation, I was charged with visiting Lepoglava - this is the biggest Croatian prison - where I saw, again, a number of these individuals. I remembered their features. And I spoke to some of them. You have to know that the Ministry of Justice insisted that the treatment according them was due and proper and transparent, that representatives of the international community should be allowed access to them, to see how they were treated and what -- what sort of conditions they were in, in prisons, and to hear any complaints they might have. What I know privately is that several of them are still serving their sentences in Lepoglava today. What their fate will be, I don't know. Another comment that I can give you, in relation to this letter is the fact that enclosed to this letter was a list of individuals, which, should, the logic dictates, be consistent and specify the names of each and every suspect that I was charged with serving papers on. So I suppose that you will find such an enclosure here. You say it says: "Enclosure, list of individuals."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just before we go to that, if you could confirm that is your signature at the foot of the page there, Mr. Penic.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the next page of the document where there is an heading: "List of suspects processed from the group of persons located in the UNCRO camp." And we see some names on the page. And is that the list that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it is or isn't, but it should be. That's what the logic dictates. Though, as I told you, I don't recall exactly the contents of the document. What I do remember is that I dictated just such a list to my secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just to point out to you, this document originates from the state archive in Zagreb, so it's a document that has been obtained from the official channels, as we can see by the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a list of names stretching over several pages. I don't propose to go through it one by one with the witness, with the Court's leave, as I don't see any purpose in that. And the witness has described the document, and Your Honours can view the full terms of it to see that it corroborates what the witness has described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections, and the Chamber is not insisting on going through the document person by person, Mr. Kay. So, therefore, you may proceed as you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I can tell the Court, again, because it is helpful, I believe. That it is signed at the end of the list of suspects by Mr. Penic himself. Also, with this document, right at the end of it, if we go to the very last page now, page 11 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where we can see your signature, Mr. Penic. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The purpose of going here is to go to the page before this now, where we'll see the heading: "Additional list of the suspects in Knin UNCRO camp." Because the evidence shows that an additional six names were -- were added to the list. We can see this now. And it's about this that I was going to ask you: Can you recollect that the original list that was formulated then had an additional list added to it of six further suspects. Can you recollect that in the chain of events?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, the document speaks for itself, and I won't go any further into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, let me ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D1941. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1941 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, to assist the Court, those members of my team have been looking at this for me, have looked at those names in the list that we've seen signed by Mr. Penic, provided them into a schedule, and then been through various court exhibits of this trial, matching the names with other documents, and providing, not with the full number of them, but, I believe, 22 -- 28 of the number, linked documents, and we will be filing that as a bar table document for the Court to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay, may I take it that that's not really evidence being presented but, rather, a document which would assist the Chamber in linking the information in this document with what we find in evidence elsewhere but in itself, then, is not to be considered as evidence, but, rather, an aide-memoire for the Court, and a document which gives some assistance to the parties -- the other parties and to the Court. Is that how we should understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've also traced the the decisions to open investigations in the files that have been produced to the Court from the Prosecution 65 ter list, and that has been incorporated. So we have this helpful schedule, I believe, but within that are the Court files that go to these particular individuals. And it's those documents that will become, with the Court's leave, first-time exhibits but linked to everything as we like to do it for the Court to try and show the connections there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, it's a mixture, to some extent. It just gives the linkages and will assist the Court in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at the same time, it also produces some material which is not in evidence yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And to that extent, therefore, it is new evidence as well. I find it important to make that distinction between assisting the Court in finding its way through what is already in evidence is something different from combining such an effort with introducing what is, for this Court, new in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will be serving that directly now that that work has been -- that task has been completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Has that been reviewed by the other parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We just received it with the cross-examination documents, so literally less than an hour ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Especially if there is new evidence involved, I'd like to give an opportunity to the other parties to consider whether there is any objection against what is produced here, because it goes beyond just assisting the Court in finding its way through what is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have no complaint. I was just linking it all up for the record, to assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I even have, helpfully prepared for me, hard-copies here to distribute this morning, which I hope will make the task easier for all concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just check whether I have any more questions, I believe I have finished --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, in those circumstances, I have finished my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Has your new material been uploaded in e-court, Mr. Kay, or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, it's all been stuff we've uncovered in the 65 ters already, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Everyone's had the information. Not us -- it's, in fact, Prosecution 65 ter material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. But you apparently got it together in a submission you want to make, the submission you want to file. Is that submission already uploaded in e-court? Because it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... it contains and refers to new evidence. So to that extent it should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It won't be a problem, Your Honour, any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Won't be a problem. Then we'll wait, for the time being, with assigning any numbers. If there is any hard copy available to the Chamber so that we can at least have a look at how you treated this material and which way you organised it, then we'll be better able to give further guidance to you and to the other parties how to proceed with this material after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for the record, some of these are not on the Prosecution 65 ter list so they make take a little bit more time to review. I haven't seen them yet. But as soon as I do, we'll try to get back to the Cermak Defence as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay provided us all with some homework. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, only two minutes. Your Honour will remember that I have three documents to be entered as bar table documents. And since I have no objections from my learned friend from the OTP, could I simply just point out on the record three documents and ask for their admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And these are all documents in relation to pardon from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there should be no disagreement about what the relevance of it is. And I take it that being aware of what these documents are, that you, Mr. Hedaraly, you have no wish to further point at specific elements in it. Under those circumstances, we'll deviate from our usual requirements for bar table filings and decide on admission of these documents. If you read one by one the 65 ter numbers, then numbers will be assigned and a decision will be taken, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The first one will be 3D00293.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D1942. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1942. The next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The next one will be 294, so 3D00294.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D1943. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1943 is admitted into evidence. Next one, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the last one will be 3D00296.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D1944. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1944 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we managed to find out the Laniste region, and we could produce it via Sanction on the screen so that you can see. It's a, let's say, two or three kilometres south from Kulen Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And now we will see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's clear. That now the line described in the document is -- is clear now. Mr. Penic, don't worry about the Laniste woods. It is -- it's relevant for us but not of direct relevance for you. There is no court in Laniste woods, was there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But I have to admit, Your Honour, that the honour goes to Ms. Prashanthi. She found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: She found it. Okay. That's on the record. And in her absence, she's praised for it. Let's proceed. Mr. Misetic are you ready to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- cross-examined Mr. Penic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Penic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Penic. I would like to start off on the issue we dealt with this morning on the Law on General Amnesty and the and/or issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So if we could call up D680, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Penic, you will recall that we were talking about Article 1 in the first paragraph, and it talks about the amnesty concerns criminal acts committed during aggression, armed conflict, or -- sorry. During aggression, armed rebellion, or armed conflicts or related to aggression, armed rebellion ... and then there's a question as to whether it should say "and" or "or armed conflicts in the Republic of Croatia." You will see in the original, as we discussed this morning, there appears to be a typographical error, so it is not clear whether in Croatian it says i, or whether it should say ili.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could now turn to Article 3, which is page 2 in the English, subparagraph 2 -- I'm sorry, page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't think that was the disagreement. I thought the disagreement was the word between the first three armed rebellion aggression and armed conflict and the second time that those words are mentioned. I don't -- at least, I didn't take it that the last -- between the armed rebellion and armed conflict, I think we agreed that that should have been an "or." At least that's how I understood the agreement. I thought it was on that Article, not on that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We found in the English version three times the word or on one line. In dispute was the middle one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have page 1 of both on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's confusing. Mr. Misetic, I was focussing on, if we read the English text, third line, reads: "... rebellion or armed conflicts, or related to ..." And it that's or, that last one, before the words "related to," which seems to be the or which was contested and understood to be and. Now as we see as the semi-last word on that line in English, again the word or, but that's not the one, neither is there -- I mean, the or, the two times or before armed seems to be not contested; whereas the or before the word related that is contested. And the Prosecution suggests that that should read "and."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And I also note for the record when Mr. Mikulicic read it for the witness as a question, the -- the interpretation that came from the booth was an and. I know that is not the determinative or final but also -- that's also on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now we know, at least, what the Prosecution argues. Mr. Misetic, please keep this in mind when putting any further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. And if that's the issue, then I don't have a problem with it, so I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there's no issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then this matter, having been settled, the Prosecution will take care of uploading a new translation, especially in relation to Article 1 of this law. Mr. Penic, we resolved the matter, even without your assistance, surprisingly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if we could now have Exhibit D1940, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise, Mr. Registrar. I meant D1809, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Penic, this is the appeal that President Tudjman issued to the Serbs in Sectors North and South on the 4th of August, 1995, which was broadcast repeatedly on Croatian TV and radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if you look at the second paragraph in both documents, both versions, you will see that President Tudjman: "... invited the members of Serbian paramilitary forces who are voluntarily or forcibly mobilised in the Serbian paramilitary forces to surrender their weapons to Croatian authority, with the guarantee they will be given amnesty according to valid Croatian laws." Now, were you, as the assistant minister of justice, aware that on the first day of Operation Storm President Tudjman had, in fact, promised rebel -- members of the Serb paramilitaries that they, in fact, would be guaranteed amnesty?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At the time, meaning on the 4th of August -- or let me rephrase that. Following this appeal, do you recall when the first time was that you heard about preparations to implement an amnesty for members of Serb paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, the preparations to implement an amnesty for members of Serb paramilitaries is something that has existed for a while. It had existed even prior to this period. It was a continuing process. Even without this appeal, the process was under way, and it was ongoing even during the military operations. I recall this very well. One could hear it round the clock on TV, in radio, for at least 48 hours. Those who wanted to listen and understand could do so easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please see Exhibit D685, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Penic, this is a European Community Monitoring Mission report from 10th of August, and -- I don't know if we have a Croatian version of this. But in the third paragraph there was a note that as of 10 August there was a meeting with an unidentified person on behalf of the Croatian government and that person: "Added that detained Krajina soldiers who have not committed war crimes will be amnestied within one month." Do you recall conversations within the first week of Operation Storm about implementing an amnesty for detained ARSK soldiers?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, do we know where this document saw the light of day?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is a report by the European Community Monitoring Mission, ECMM, about meetings that they had on the 10th of August -- on or about the 10th of August with officials of the Croatian government. And this records that an official of the Croatian government stated that detained Krajina soldiers who have not committed war crimes will be amnestied within one month. Now, do you recall within the first week of Operation Storm discussions within the Ministry of Justice that detained ARSK soldiers would be amnestied, if they had not committed war crimes?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I recall that. There were conversations to that effect. And when I was in Knin at the camp, I mentioned the same thing in the broader context. I said that all those who were supposed to be kept in custody and who would eventually be found not guilty of having committed war crimes would be set free. This was a well-known fact. I and all those from the Ministry of Justice used every opportunity to interpret this decision and convey it to those in the field. I don't know, though, whether I am the person referred to in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what was your understanding of why amnesties were being considered and, ultimately, amnesties and pardons implemented?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: I can explain that from a number of different aspects; my personal aspect, my professional aspect, and the way I saw it as a Croatian citizen and a person who had personal tragedies concerning my family in Vukovar, some of whom were captured and killed. It is crystal clear to me that this pardon had to take place, for without it, there would never have been any sort of peace, be it in the Danubian region or elsewhere. My colleagues and I were deeply convinced that it needs to take place. Although, as I mentioned already, we were all highly sensitive about that issue. It very difficult to forgive at the time when Croatia was in flames. Still, the pardon did take place. I personally participated in the process; I disseminated the idea in the field; and I personally believed that we could not move forward without it. It was a basic step to take so as to enable Croatia to move on. I don't know whether this answers your question, but this would be my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It does, Mr. Penic, and I wanted to hear your answer first before I show you the meeting that took place - and this is Exhibit D681 - between President Tudjman and Mrs. Elisabeth Rehn. And President Tudjman's explanation - and this begins at page -- transcript page 6523, beginning at line 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn to page 2 in Exhibit D681.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. Penic, I only have it in English because the conversation was in English. But President Tudjman says: "We in Croatia ... wanted to avoid everything that took place ... and we propose that after Tito this Yugoslav crisis by peaceful means on a confederal basis ..." He goes on: "... Croatia and then Bosnia suffered such an aggression, I don't know if you visited Vukovar or not. But a third of Croatia was destroyed. 400.000 Croats, Hungarians, Czechs, Slovaks were forced out of their homes. And naturally people were" -- I believe it should say "... murdered. It is understood that in the course of the liberation of these areas, on the Croatian side, it was also impossible to constrain the fighting to fighting in gloves." And he goes on: "Therefore, first of all, the Yugo-Communist army and the Serbs committed terrible crimes in such an aggression, aimed at creating Greater Serbia. And later, in the liberation of these areas, it was also impossible to prevent people who had suffered and who were now returning to those areas from committing acts of revenge and stupidity such as destroying homes and so forth. Therefore it is important now to forget all of this as soon as possible and to build normal relations among people, among nations, rather, even though it is necessary to punish individuals for war crimes. If we went to this breadth, if we were to approach this issue so broadly, this would mean a new deepening of mistrust and conflict. So it is more important that we develop a new order and establish trust." Now, Mr. Penic, your prior answer to my question also suggested that it was -- your view was that the amnesty needed to take place so that Croatia could move on. Was this, in fact, the general view from President Tudjman down to your level as Assistant Minister that this amnesty needed to be passed so that reconciliation could take place?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. As the secretary of the state commission for pardons, I had the opportunity to acquaint President Tudjman with some of the decisions. I will never forget his sentence when he said one needs to forget. I served a prison sentence, but I'm not sure how much it changed me. I didn't have much opportunity to meet with him personally, but these were his words. If you're asking me about my impression, when he says stupidity, such as destroying homes, I am quite certain that he didn't have war crimes in mind either. He, as well as the entire top state -- state top and the public and all those people of goodwill always rejected war crimes as something that is not accepted in civilisational terms, something that should not be put aside. This was a general position at the time, and I believe it is still is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to turn your attention to what happened after the amnesty law was passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could please go to Exhibit D682.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you will see, Mr. Penic, that this is a Security Council report on the situation of human rights in Croatia, and it's dated 5 March 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to paragraph 24, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "In the region at present, administered by UNTAES," which is eastern Slavonia, "the application of the amnesty law continues to cause widespread concern among the Serb population. At the time of writing of the present report, the Croatian authorities were preparing a definitive list of persons believed by them to be in the region and who, in the eyes of the Ministry of Justice, are not covered by the amnesty law. All those not on the list may then consider themselves as amnestied." And then it says: "At the request of UNTAES, on 27 February, the deputy minister of justice of Croatia publicly announced that such lists," meaning unofficial lists, "had been prepared by unauthorised persons, had not been prepared by the government or the judiciary, and were not valid. He stated that the final list of war crimes suspects would be released as soon as possible."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says in the middle of the paragraph: "The Croatian government has a clear interest in detaining and prosecuting persons reasonably suspected of war crimes. However, appeals have been made to the government, including by the Special Rapporteur of the Commission on Human Rights to finalise its lists of war crimes suspects on the basis of existing evidence, to remove uncertainty, and ensure that arbitrary arrests are not made among Serbs returning to Croatia." And let me just call your attention, this Trial Chamber has heard testimony, beginning at page 24812, at line 19, if I -- that as part of this process of preparing lists, Croatia was urged to reduce the number of people on the list from 150 to 85, and then, ultimately was urged by the international community to reduce that list further to 25 Serbs who would be on this list, and then everyone not on the list would be considered amnestied. Now, my question, Mr. Penic, is the reference in the Security Council report as to the deputy minister of justice addressing this issue of the lists, were you the deputy minister referred to in this report?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: It resembles the description of my title but any public appearances were prohibited to me. If this was a statement of a public official, then it is not myself. As for the drafting of such lists and registers, the customary model used by the ministry and my administration was that we would send a circular letter to all the Courts in Croatia asking for coming up with all the documents they have and to make a specific list of all criminal proceedings and procedures they had instituted. And we did this over and over again, because we wanted to have the most recent information about proceedings for war crimes, not only against Serbs but everyone else. We did not distinguish between ethnic groups. We kept registers of all war crimes in general. In that respect, I recall well, and I mentioned that in my statement to Mr. Mikulicic, no matter how little I recall it, there must be registers in the Ministry of Justice. This is the model we followed. As for the reduction of the number of people concerned, we did gather information. We did systematise information. And I know that the list was reduced. But I did not take part in it directly. It was done by the state top in the course of talks and negotiations I'm not privy to. Obviously they wished to stabilise the situation as soon as possible, and they did some of those things without consulting the profession. I believe they reduced the number of crimes, although I personally would not have. It was their view, and they did it in good faith. That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, as a result of the creation of these lists, whether the amnesty law was supposed to be interpreted in such a way that those -- anyone who -- any Serb who was not on the list of 25 would be considered amnestied, including, amnestied for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: All those who were not on the war crimes list, this was supposed to be the interpretation, that all others would be included in the amnesty. So everyone, save for those who had committed war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you say "save for those who committed war crimes," do you mean specifically those that were identified on the list of 25?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Well, the quality of evidence, as far as I could see as a professional and person who worked for a number of years as a Deputy State Prosecutor, was based on a realistic prosecutorial assessment about the quality of evidence they had at their disposal. All case files, I believe there were around 45 or so which pertained to war crimes, I presume, although I was not familiar with individual cases, had quality and sound arguments to corroborate such charges. If someone was pardoned, despite having committed war crimes, is something I -- that is something I cannot comment on. But the logic dictates that such instances did happen under the pressure of the international community, which probably carried out an analysis of their own, having finally concluded that the -- there was not enough evidence of someone in particular having committed war crimes. And according to the principle in dubio pro reo, they asked that a number of cases be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just want to be clear on this, and this is my last question. And I apologise to the Chamber if it's repetitive, but I want to be clear. Was it your understanding as assistant minister of justice that once these lists, or this list, was finalised in terms of the persons on the list, that those persons who were not on the list would be covered by the general amnesty, even if there was a allegation that such a person not on the list had committed war crimes?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Penic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Penic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Hedaraly is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Penic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can go to D680 again. That was the Law on General Pardon that we have discussed now a few times, that you have discussed a few times. And the Article I want to focus on is Article 3, which are the crimes that are excluded from the -- from the amnesty law. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And we see here that there are -- it goes from Article 119 of the basic Criminal Code up to and including Article 137; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can just pull up D1627 now, which is the basic Criminal Code, or the basic criminal law of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When we are waiting for it, I noticed, Mr. Hedaraly, that you are using the word the Law on General Pardon where the text -- the title of the law is translated as Law on General Amnesty. I also noticed that in some of the decisions that pardon is granted in relation to persons that have not yet been convicted. If you look at it from a comparative view, then I just want to put on the record that the use of the word "amnesty," "pardon," is not very consistent in this respect. And since you are mixing them up, even using another term, I would like to put that on the record, that "pardon" should not be necessarily understood as what pardon is considered to be, for example, in France or ... Because often what is called pardon here would be called amnesty by others; whereas, sometimes amnesty may have been called pardon. So I just wanted to make sure that we are dealing with a -- an animal under several names and an animal both striped sometimes and sometimes of another colour. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And we saw the -- I'm sorry. The list from Article 119 to Article 127, where the war crimes listed there. And if we go in the law -- if we go to page 32 of the B/C/S. And, Your Honours, the whole translation was not uploaded, only selected portions. The portion I want to deal with has been uploaded separately. And if we can ask Mr. Registrar to call that under doc ID 0606-8913-EDT, that will be the chapter 15, which covers the articles I just mentioned and that I want to go through. And I will then ask to link the translation with the -- with the exhibit that is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So we see here, Mr. Penic, Article 119 begins the section in chapter 15 that is called "Crimes Against Humanity and International Law." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we go to the Article 137, which is the last one listed in the Article 3 of the Law on Amnesty --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which is page 36 of the B/C/S, and I think it's page 18 in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is page 10, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And we see that after Article 137, which is the last one, we start chapter 16 which is a different section. So the entire section on war crimes and crimes against international law is covered in chapter 15 and is referenced in Article 3 of the Law on Amnesty. Correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And all those crimes are concluded from the amnesty law?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if which go to Article 120 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can move back to page 32 in the B/C/S and page 1 of the English, of the new translation. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You see Article 120 is headed: "War Crime Against a Civilian Population."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn to the next page in the English only, and it's in the first paragraph in the B/C/S, the last four or five lines. The English, one of the war crimes that is listed is: "... property be confiscated or that the property of the population be looted or that the property be unlawfully and wantonly destroyed or seized and large-scale without this being justified by military needs." And it goes on. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So that means that looting and burning as a war crime was also excluded from the amnesty law; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we can just go back to D680 now, which was the Law on Amnesty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if we could have permission to link that translation that was uploaded to D1627, which is an admitted exhibit, we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? Mr. Registrar, this portion of the translation can be linked to -- let me just check. One second, please. D1627. Mr. Registrar, could you confirm that this will be linked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document ID English translation 0606-8913-ET will be attached to Exhibit D1627. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if we could go to the second page of both the B/C/S and the English, this time Article 3 but the second paragraph. And I believe here, once again, Mr. President, we have the issue of the "and" and the "or" in the second to last line. But we will -- the whole document will be revised so it's the same language in the original from the -- from Article 1. But, Mr. Penic, my question is: According to this paragraph, any crime -- any other crime that did not fall within that category of being during the armed conflict, aggression, and rebellion, and in connection to it, would also be excluded from the Law on Amnesty; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Yes. These would be offences of a classical crime committed by classical or conventional criminals, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my understanding, Mr. Hedaraly, if you positively define conditions and you use the word "and," isn't it true that if you then exempt, make exceptions, that you should make an exception with the word or? And here I read that the word is, apparently, "ili," which is -- or if I say in order to get paid you have to appear at work and you have to wear a robe, now, if I want to accept this from payment, then you say, If you do not appear or do not wear a robe, you will not be paid. So in a positive formulation, where "and" is used, doesn't mean that in a negative exemptive clause that you would also have to use "and." I think, as a matter of fact, that there you would properly use the word "or."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, I think the whole sentence and the whole Article and the translation that I had actually specifically identifies the two conditions and accepts them, and that's why there may be an "and." But when we get the complete revision, it's going to be clear. Although I do see Your Honour's point, and I think that the witness understands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it reads "which were not committed there, or which are not related to." There, the "or" makes sense, where the "and" makes sense in a positive formulation. I just wanted to -- before we start getting nuts and bolts loosened from translations, that there is a -- maybe a difference here. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure if this is along your point, but the form of the question, the initial question, was that if it did not fall within that category of being during the armed conflict aggression and rebellion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is the -- one of the other ors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. I think it should be "or rebellion."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would please rephrase your question because Mr. Penic might have lost track of what he has asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Crimes that were not -- that did not take place during the armed conflict and, at the same time, that were not in connection with the armed conflict, so only one of the two conditions may have been satisfied. For example, it may have occurred during the armed conflict but not in connection with it. Just a temporal scope, if only that would have been the case, that would have been excluded by the amnesty law. Correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: If I may, I will give you the following answer: It is only the legislature who can interpret the law. I cannot; I can only read it. In my reading of it, well, it can be read on the Internet site of the Official Gazette of the Republic of Croatia. My reading of it is as follows: The intention was to punish both those who were in the armed rebellion and those who were in the armed conflicts. In other words, in answer to your question, they could have been published for or or and for and and, cumulatively and separately. At any rate, both those who did something in the armed rebellion and in connection with the aggression could fall under it and those who did something in relation to or related to the armed rebellion. I don't know how far this takes us in terms of bus being muddled up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that we should take our 19 hours to think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I actually don't have any further questions so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have any further questions. Then you have three minutes to further revolve this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let's take your -- the example that Mr. President gave earlier. If there was a common crime that took place during the rebellion or the conflict or any of the -- the aggression, if there was a crime that took place that had nothing to do with the armed conflict as such, it was a neighbour stealing a neighbour's cow or killing his neighbour for reasons unrelated to the armed conflict, would that be subject to the amnesty law, that crime?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PENIC
utterances.text: Let me answer this way: In application of this law, a case law developed. It was the courts who applied the laws and regulations. It was the courts who, on a case to case basis, had to make an assessment of whether something was done under the garb of darkness or criminal conduct. If I did the most common -- the commonest of crimes, if I committed a crime outside of armed activities, and if I did something because I knew that property would be abandoned as a result of the war And war activities, then I committed something that was related to the war conflict. What had to clarify the whole matter was the developing case law. I believe the nuances were not so difficult to distinguish. The existence of war circumstances enabling a common citizen to become a criminal is something, in my view, if you're asking for my opinion, that should be in interpreted as crime committed in the aggression or related to aggression. That same individual, perhaps, barring these war circumstances, would not have committed the offence. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Penic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any need for re-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Penic, since the Chamber has no further questions for you, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I would like to thank you very much for coming the long way to The Hague and/or for answering all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please follow Mr. Usher, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest to the parties that we deal finally tomorrow with the list which is submitted by Mr. Kay, that is, the bar table documents. Mr. Kay, do I understand well, that, for example, on your list, the second, third, and fourth person are covered by that one decision to open an investigation so that it includes three persons, which would then mean that, for example, for two, three, and four we would need one exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Registrar, you are invited to provisionally assign, and we'll hear from you tomorrow, exhibit numbers in accordance with the 65 ter numbers; that is, one 65 ter number resulting in one provisional exhibit number. Then I would like to hear from the other parties whether there is any objection against the way in which it is presented, including the linkage to other exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Provided it's accurate. And we will review it. There are no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same for the other parties. And then, finally, I have not yet had an opportunity to see what the reasons were for P1039 to be under seal, whether that creates any further problems. We will deal with this matter tomorrow. The Chamber will give an opportunity to the parties to make their further submissions on the still outstanding matter which is involvement in interviewing witnesses by persons who may be -- may be linked in whatever way to events that happened at the time. Prosecution asked for 15 minutes. We'll deal with that in the first session. And then, as matters stand now, it may well be that there will be sufficient time to do the housekeeping session as well. Yesterday I have prepared the -- myself for the latest MFI list. Which, if it is not yet distributed, will be distributed this afternoon so that we know what we are talking about. Mr. Mikulicic, you are on your feet. Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was just -- I would like to inform the Chamber that we will, during this afternoon, submit our bar table submission relating to General Repinc's testimony. And probably we could discuss it tomorrow, if there would be no objections from the OTP side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everyone is invited to look at it, and then we'll see whether we can deal with it tomorrow. We are put on notice. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 20th of January, 9.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 20th of January, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
